intro: Two samples can differ by a small shift even when none of their values match. Wasserstein distance measures how far probability mass must move.
task: Compute the one-dimensional Wasserstein-1 distance between two equally weighted empirical distributions of potentially different sample sizes.
requirements: first and second are nonempty vectors. Every observation has mass 1/len(its_vector), including duplicates.
Integrate the absolute difference between the two empirical CDFs across consecutive distinct pooled observation values.
Return a nonnegative scalar. Sample lengths may differ; do not zip sorted arrays unless their lengths happen to match.

Use real finite numeric inputs with magnitude at most 1e6, excluding booleans. Vectors have length 1..128 and matrix axes have length 1..128 unless a tighter bound is stated. Leave all inputs unchanged; raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Find the structure
hints.body: The CDFs change only at pooled sample values, so integrate over intervals between adjacent distinct values.

hints.title: Build the calculation
hints.body: Evaluate both inclusive CDFs at each left endpoint and multiply their absolute difference by that interval width.

explanation: Between adjacent pooled sample values, each empirical CDF is constant. The area between the two CDFs is therefore a sum of rectangle widths times probability differences.

Equal sample sizes permit matching sorted observations, but unequal sizes require splitting mass. The CDF formulation handles both cases and preserves duplicate observations as repeated probability mass.
